newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Clinton sends reassuring signals to China.
newsitem.headline: Clinton sends reassuring signals to China.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton, following talks with Australian Prime Minister John Howard, said on Wednesday he opposed isolating China and insisted engaging Beijing was a "big priority for all of us".
Clinton's comments were clearly aimed at reassuring Beijing and followed a meeting with Howard which senior U.S. officials said included a detailed discussion of relations with China.
The Chinese have been growing fearful that Washington has resurrected its old Cold War strategy of containment to isolate the communist giant.
"I think China has to be a big priority for all of us," Clinton said during a joint news conference with Howard in Australia's national parliament house.

Clinton said any list of the "five big questions" that will determine the shape of the world 50 years from now would have to include: "How will the Chinese define their greatness in the 21st Century?"

"Will they find their greatness in terms of the incredible potential of their people to learn, to produce, to succeed economically and culturally...or will they define their greatness in terms of their ability to dominate their neighbours and others against their will?" Clinton asked.
Striking a reassuring tone in advance of his planned meeting in the Philippines on Sunday with Chinese President Jiang Zemin, Clinton said: "The United States has no interest in containing China".

"That is a negative strategy. What the United States wants is to sustain an engagement with China...in a way that will increase the chances that there will be more liberty and more prosperity," Clinton said.

Clinton meets with China's leader before the start of a round of talks on trade issues at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum. He also plans talks on Sunday with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and South Korean President Kim Young-sam.
Clinton also reaffirmed Washington's military commitment to maintaining stability in the Asia-Pacific region, citing a decision for 2,500 U.S. marines to train in northern Australia.
"They are seriously a powerful symbol and a concrete manifestation of our place to protect stability in the Pacific," said Clinton.

In July, Washington and Canberra signed a defence agreement aimed at bolstering security ties by upgrading joint U.S.-Australia military facilities, the establishment of a small marine base in Australia and boosting joint training.
The move prompted Beijing to accuse Australia of being used by Washington as part of a containment pincer with Japan.
Australia has rejected the charge. "The Australian government does not pursue a policy of the containment of China," Downer told parliament on Tuesday.
"Suggestions...that Australia and the United States, through the Sydney declaration and the alliance we have, is somehow directed towards China is an analysis which is simply wrong."
In a later address to a joint sitting of the Australian parliament, Clinton was expected to reaffirm Washington's commitment to the Asia-Pacific region.

"I know that some people on both sides of the Pacific are concerned that America's continuing engagement with Europe will lead to disengagement from Asia," Clinton said in remarks prepared for delivery to parliament. "They are wrong."
Borrowing a phrase used by Howard to describe his foreign policy attitudes, Clinton said "the U.S. need not choose between our history and our geography. We need not choose between Europe and Asia."
"In a global economy with global security challenges, America must look to the East no less than it looks to the West."
